{{Short description|Analog of Grothendieck topology}}
In mathematics, a '''Lawvere–Tierney topology''' is an analog of a [[Grothendieck topology]] for an arbitrary [[elementary topos]], used to construct a topos of sheaves. A Lawvere–Tierney topology is also sometimes also called a '''local operator''' or '''coverage''' or '''topology''' or '''geometric modality'''. They were introduced  by {{harvs|txt|authorlink=William Lawvere|last=Lawvere|first=William|year=1971}} and [[Myles Tierney]].

==Definition==

If ''E'' is a topos, then a topology on ''E'' is a morphism ''j'' from the [[subobject classifier]] Ω to Ω such that ''j'' preserves truth (<math>j \circ \mbox{true} = \mbox{true}</math>), preserves intersections (<math>j \circ \wedge = \wedge \circ (j \times j)</math>), and is idempotent (<math>j \circ j = j</math>).

==''j''-closure==
[[Image:J-closure.png|right|400px|thumb|Commutative diagrams showing how ''j''-closure operates. &Omega; and ''t'' are the [[subobject classifier]]. &chi;<sub>s</sub> is the characteristic morphism of ''s'' as a subobject of ''A'' and <math>j \circ \chi_s</math> is the characteristic morphism of <math>\bar s</math> which is the ''j''-closure of ''s''. The bottom two squares are pullback squares and they are contained in the top diagram as well: the first one as a trapezoid and the second one as a two-square rectangle.]]
Given a subobject <math>s:S \rightarrowtail A</math> of an object ''A'' with classifier <math>\chi_s:A \rightarrow \Omega</math>, then the composition <math>j \circ \chi_s</math> defines another subobject <math>\bar s:\bar S \rightarrowtail A</math> of ''A'' such that ''s'' is a subobject of <math>\bar s</math>, and <math>\bar s</math> is said to be the ''j''-[[closure operator|closure]] of ''s''.

Some theorems related to ''j''-closure are (for some subobjects ''s'' and ''w'' of ''A''):
* inflationary property: <math>s \subseteq \bar s</math>
* idempotence: <math>\bar s \equiv \bar \bar s</math>
* preservation of intersections: <math>\overline{s \cap w} \equiv \bar s \cap \bar w </math>
* preservation of order: <math>s \subseteq w \Longrightarrow \bar s \subseteq \bar w</math>
* stability under pullback: <math> \overline{f^{-1}(s)} \equiv f^{-1}(\bar s)</math>.

==Examples==

* Grothendieck topologies on a small category ''C'' are essentially the same as Lawvere–Tierney topologies on the topos of presheaves of sets over ''C''.
* Lawvere–Tierney topologies on the [[effective topos]] generalize the notion of an [[oracle (computability)|oracle]] in [[computability theory]].{{r|kihara}}

==Internal point of view==

The statement that a morphism <math>j : \Omega \to \Omega</math> is a Lawvere–Tierney topology can be expressed purely in the [[internal language]] of the elementary topos. Indeed, a rephrasing of the definition is that <math>j</math> is a Lawvere–Tierney topology when the following three conditions are satisfied internally:

# <math>j(\top) = \top</math>
# <math>\forall \, p : \Omega, j(j(p)) \Leftrightarrow j(p)</math>
# <math>\forall \, p \, q : \Omega, j(p \land q) \Leftrightarrow j(p) \land j(q)</math>

An equivalent definition uses the following three conditions instead:{{r|nlab}}

# <math>\forall \, p \, q : \Omega, (p \Rightarrow q) \Rightarrow (j(p) \Rightarrow j(q))</math>
# <math>\forall \, p : \Omega, p \Rightarrow j(p)</math>
# <math>\forall \, p : \Omega, j(j(p)) \Rightarrow j(p)</math>

This reveals that a Lawvere–Tierney topology is the same as a [[monad (category theory)|monad]] on the set of truth values <math>\Omega</math> partially ordered by implication, viewed as a [[posetal category]]. In particular, another equivalent definition is by the following conditions, which follow the standard convention of defining [[Monad (functional programming)|monads in functional programming]] by the <code>ret</code> and <code>bind</code> operators:

# <math>\forall \, p : \Omega, p \Rightarrow j(p)</math>
# <math>\forall \, p \, q : \Omega, (p \Rightarrow j(q)) \Rightarrow (j(p) \Rightarrow j(q))</math>

The second condition can be informally stated as: to prove a proposition of the form <math>j(q)</math>, one can without loss of generality replace any hypothesis <math>j(p)</math> with just <math>p</math>.
